real_world_anchor.primary: A straight track has a starting post and one heading. After that, a single number — how far along you are — names every place on it. Delivered verbatim in STATE_1's narration and cashed by the extending line and the live lambda marker. Universal — a straight track exists everywhere, and the claim is only that one number names a position on it.
real_world_anchor.secondary: On a flat map two straight roads cross. On the ground one runs over the other, and they never touch. Assigned to STATE_5, where the skew case is taught, so the reveal is not spoiled earlier. Universal — a road overpass exists everywhere, and the claim is only that two straight things can look like they cross while passing at different depths.

lambda_span.name: half-length each drawn line extends either side of its anchor (STATE_9 only)

theta_deg.name: angle between the two skew directions d1 and d2

formulas.point_plane_distance: D = |n_hat . (q - a)| / |n| (capital D: the distance; lowercase d is reserved concept-wide for line directions)
formulas.line_plane_meet: lambda = n . (a_plane - a_line) / (n . d), undefined (no meeting point) when n . d = 0
formulas.skew_distance: D = |(a2 - a1) . (d1 x d2)| / |d1 x d2| (capital D: the distance; lowercase d1/d2 are the two directions)

constraints: every relation this concept draws is defined everywhere it is drawn: a line has no excluded lambda, a plane has no excluded point, and the point-plane distance is defined for every q not on the plane -- the only real exclusion is the DEGENERATE case a line-plane meet or a common-perpendicular direction fails to exist, and both are DETECTED (an inequality test on a dot/cross product of unit vectors, epsilon 1e-9) rather than divided-by-zero

the degeneracy epsilon (1e-9) gates BOTH the line-meets-plane test and the common-perpendicular-exists test as an inequality, never an exact-zero test, so a line authored exactly parallel by construction (float round-off of order 1e-16) is still correctly classified parallel

n . d for the STATE_4/STATE_7 cutting line renders as 0.574 on the live HUD (both operands normalized by the renderer before the dot product), matching cos(55deg) = sin(35deg) exactly -- never 0.624, which is a different, un-rendered quantity (a unit direction dotted with the un-normalized plane-normal vector)

the STATE_5 screen-crossing marker is authored as a literal 3D point on the first skew line at (-1.797411, -0.989612, 0.390906), independently re-derived from the STATE_5 camera pose (radius 13, azimuth 146deg, elevation 4deg) by solving the two lines' projected screen paths for their intersection in closed form

STATE_1's entry camera_position is [0.0, 8.0, 13.8564] (radius 16, azimuth 90deg, elevation 30deg) -- the sibling concept vector_products_in_space's own STATE_5 camera literal, verbatim -- and its within-state camera_steps eases IN to radius 13, not out

half_extent's slider ceiling must be widened past the shared default (which tops out at 3.0) to reach this concept's own domain ceiling of 4.5 on STATE_9, via a per-state control_ranges override -- otherwise STATE_9's own solved camera pose (framed for the full 1.5-4.5 sweep) is not actually reachable by a live drag

theta_deg's on-screen angle-arc fidelity is authored ONLY over [25, 115] degrees -- STATE_6 and STATE_9's skew-view row both narrow theta_deg to that interval via control_ranges, never left at a wider shared default

the STATE_2 two-segment dot-product-introduction recipe relies on both segments reading n . v = 0 for every value of their own driving knob whenever both of a segment's endpoints are in-plane addresses -- this holds unconditionally, which is what keeps the per-frame readout from ever printing a wrong value during either segment's idle window

aha_moment.statement: Of every segment from a point to a plane, the perpendicular one is shortest.
aha_moment.visual_confirmation: The sweeping segment's live length falls to 2.20 and rises again on either side; only the perpendicular segment locks green with a right-angle mark at that minimum.

tts_sentences.text_en: Naming a plane needs one more idea: a perpendicular direction, called the normal.
A vector in the plane gives zero dot product — also called scalar product — with the normal.
Tip it out of the plane, and the reading leaves zero.
The plane is named. Take a point off it: how far is it?

STATE_3.title: The Perpendicular Is the Shortest Segment

misconception_watch.belief: The distance from a point to a plane is just how far it is to the nearest bit of the plane you can see — any segment down to it will do.
misconception_watch.visual_counter: The sweeping segment shows several different lengths for the same point — 3.11 at one landing spot, 2.72 at another — and only stops falling when it turns perpendicular, locking at 2.20.
misconception_watch.one_line_fix: Every segment from the point to the plane is longer than the perpendicular one, so the perpendicular length is the distance.

It reaches its smallest value at the perpendicular, and locks.
That perpendicular is the distance. Replace the point with a line: does it reach the plane, or miss it?

STATE_4.title: A Line Meets a Plane Once, or Never

misconception_watch.belief: n · d = 0 means the line is perpendicular to the plane.
misconception_watch.visual_counter: The line with n·d = 0 is shown doing what that condition actually forces: it glides past the plane, staying perpendicular to the normal the whole time (90 degrees), and never touches it. The line that does cut through reads n·d = 0.574, plainly not zero.
misconception_watch.one_line_fix: n · d = 0 means the direction is perpendicular to the normal, which puts the line parallel to the plane.

Its height never changes, so it never touches.
A second line arrives, heading differently. It crosses, and a marker appears.
A line meets a plane in two ways. Two lines in space have a third case, one only three dimensions allow.

misconception_watch.belief: If two lines are not parallel, they must cross somewhere.

misconception_watch.one_line_fix: Their pictures cross, but at that place they are 1.80 apart along the line joining them — in space, not parallel does not mean meeting.

tts_sentences.text_en: On a flat map, two straight roads cross.
On the ground, one runs over the other, and they never touch.
These two lines cross on screen, but not in space.
These are called skew lines: not parallel, and never meeting.
The true gap lies between their nearest points.
The angle must come from directions alone.

misconception_watch.belief: The angle between two lines can be more than 90 degrees
misconception_watch.visual_counter: The second line keeps turning past perpendicular, but the angle readout rises to 90.0° and then falls back to 65.0°
misconception_watch.one_line_fix: The angle between two lines is the smaller of the two angles they make, so it is never more than 90°; that is why the formula takes the absolute value of d₁·d₂.

Slide one line along itself: the angle does not change.

assessment.mastery_definition: A student has mastered this concept when they can name a point on a line as the anchor plus a multiple of the direction; use the dot product with the normal as the test for lying in a plane; state that the distance from a point to a plane is measured along the perpendicular, never any other segment; classify a line-plane pair as meeting once or never from the sign of n·d; recognise that two non-parallel, non-meeting lines in space are skew rather than intersecting; and state that the angle between two lines depends only on their directions, never on where they are placed.

questions.stem: A line passes through the point a in the direction d. Which of these points lies on the line?

distractor_misconceptions.B: Swaps the anchor and the direction, as if either vector could play either role.
distractor_misconceptions.C: Scales the anchor point the same way lambda scales the direction, when only the direction moves.
distractor_misconceptions.D: Drops the anchor entirely, treating the direction alone as if it already named a place.

questions.tested_idea: a point on a line is the anchor plus a multiple of the direction
questions.parallel_form_stem: A line passes through the point p in the direction u. Which point lies on the line for lambda = 3?

questions.stem: A plane passes through the point a with normal n. Which condition means a vector v lies IN the plane?

distractor_misconceptions.B: Mistakes zero alignment for some fixed non-zero reading, rather than the perpendicularity test itself.
distractor_misconceptions.C: Confuses the perpendicularity test with parallel directions, which is what a zero cross product means instead.
distractor_misconceptions.D: Compares lengths instead of directions — the test is about angle, not magnitude.

questions.tested_idea: the dot product with the normal is the test for lying in the plane
questions.parallel_form_stem: A plane has normal m. A vector w satisfies m · w = 0. What does that tell you about w?

questions.stem: The distance from a point to a plane is measured:

options.A: along the perpendicular from the point to the plane
options.B: along the shortest visible line to the edge of the plane
options.C: along any straight line from the point that reaches the plane
options.D: along the line joining the point to the plane's own anchor point

distractor_misconceptions.B: Reads 'shortest' as 'nearest edge on screen' rather than as the perpendicular length.
distractor_misconceptions.C: Believes any segment reaching the plane measures 'the' distance, when only one segment gives the minimum.
distractor_misconceptions.D: Picks the anchor point as if it were always the closest point on the plane, which is true only by coincidence.

questions.tested_idea: distance to a plane is measured along the perpendicular, not any connecting segment

questions.stem: A line has n · d = 0, and its own point is not on the plane. The line and the plane:

distractor_misconceptions.B: Reads n·d = 0 as the line being perpendicular to the plane, when it means the line is parallel to it.
distractor_misconceptions.C: Assumes every line and plane must cross somewhere, missing the parallel case entirely.
distractor_misconceptions.D: Confuses 'parallel and never touching' with 'lying inside', which would need every point of the line to satisfy the plane's own equation.

questions.tested_idea: n·d = 0 means the direction is perpendicular to the normal, so the line is parallel to the plane

questions.stem: Two lines in space are not parallel and share no common point. They are:

options.C: parallel by definition, since they never meet
options.D: not a possible configuration in three dimensions

distractor_misconceptions.B: Carries plane geometry into space, where not-parallel no longer forces a meeting point.
distractor_misconceptions.C: Confuses 'never meets' with the definition of parallel, when parallel additionally requires the same direction.
distractor_misconceptions.D: Believes every pair of lines must fall into the two plane-geometry cases, missing the genuinely three-dimensional case.

questions.tested_idea: not parallel and no common point means skew, a case that only exists in three dimensions

questions.stem: Does sliding one of two lines along its own direction change the angle between them?

options.A: no — the angle depends only on the two directions
options.B: yes, because the crossing point moves
options.C: yes, but only if the lines are skew
options.D: no — but only because the example angle happens to be a round number

distractor_misconceptions.B: Believes the angle depends on where the lines meet on screen, when the angle is computed from directions alone.
distractor_misconceptions.C: Believes intersecting lines are governed by different rules than skew lines, when both use the same direction-only measurement.
distractor_misconceptions.D: Treats the invariance as a coincidence of this particular angle, rather than as true for any two directions.

questions.tested_idea: the angle between two lines is fixed by their directions alone, independent of position

questions.stem: A point sits 3 units from a plane, measured along the perpendicular. A slanted segment from the same point to the plane measures:

options.D: it depends on which direction the segment leans

distractor_misconceptions.B: Assumes every segment to a flat plane reads the same length.
distractor_misconceptions.C: Reverses the inequality — believes a slanted path is shorter than the straight perpendicular one.
distractor_misconceptions.D: Treats the length as direction-dependent in a way that could beat the minimum, when the perpendicular is always shortest.

questions.tested_idea: every non-perpendicular segment from the point to the plane is longer than the perpendicular one
